topic: Special Hosts — Sepsis in the Immunocompromised
speakerTitle: Consultant in Infectious Diseases & Acute Medicine
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Infection & Immunocompromised Host Unit
speakerBio: Infectious-diseases physician who runs the neutropenic-sepsis pathway and the splenectomy vaccination clinic, with a special interest in infection in the transplant recipient.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 41-year-old woman, day 10 after her third cycle of chemotherapy for breast cancer, phones the triage line: "I feel a bit off, maybe a temperature." She walks into the emergency department, chatting, pink, observations almost normal — a single reading of 38.1°C. The junior doctor thinks "viral, send her home." Ninety minutes later she is hypotensive and periarrest. She has neutropenic sepsis, and her immune system is the reason she looked so well. Tonight is about the septic patient whose defences are broken — and whose broken defences hide the very fire that is killing them.

1 · ⚠️ The governing principle — the signs are switched off

Every clinical sign of sepsis you were taught — the fever spike, the leukocytosis, the pus, the consolidation, the peritonism — is produced by a competent inflammatory response. Take away the neutrophils, the spleen, or the T-cells and you take away the signs, not the danger. The immunocompromised septic patient is sicker than they look, and deteriorating faster than a normal host.

In the immunocompromised, absence of signs is not absence of sepsis — it is absence of an immune system.
💡 The three broken defences

Neutrophils (chemotherapy, marrow failure) → bacterial and fungal sepsis with no pus. Spleen (splenectomy, sickle cell, coeliac) → fulminant encapsulated-organism sepsis. T-cells/macrophages (transplant, steroids, biologics, HIV) → opportunistic and reactivated pathogens. Identify which door is open and you predict the bug.

2 · 🩸 Neutropenic sepsis / febrile neutropenia — a medical emergency

Definition: temperature >38.0°C (or a single reading ≥38.3°C, or sustained >38.0°C for 1 h) plus an absolute neutrophil count (ANC) <0.5 ×10⁹/L — or <1.0 and predicted to fall below 0.5. Note: fever may be the only sign, and in the profoundly neutropenic even fever can be absent (look for hypothermia, hypotension, new confusion, mucositis).

Risk is stratified by the depth and duration of neutropenia. ANC <0.1 for >7 days (e.g. induction AML, allogeneic transplant) is the highest-risk group and where invasive fungal disease emerges.

The one rule that saves lives

Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within ONE HOUR of presentation — cultures should not delay the first dose.

First-line is an anti-pseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy:

AgentNote
Piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV q6–8hCommon first-line
Meropenem 1 g IV q8hIf prior ESBL, severe sepsis, or CNS source
Cefepime 2 g IV q8hAlternative anti-pseudomonal cephalosporin
CeftazidimeAlternative (weaker Gram-positive cover)
⚠️ Do not routinely add vancomycin up front

IDSA does not recommend adding a glycopeptide to the empiric regimen for every febrile neutropenic patient — it does not improve outcomes and drives resistance and nephrotoxicity. Add vancomycin/teicoplanin only for a specific indication: haemodynamic instability, suspected line/catheter infection, skin/soft-tissue infection, severe mucositis, MRSA colonisation, or Gram-positive cocci in blood before sensitivities. Review and stop it at 48–72 h if not needed.

MASCC score — who can go home?

The MASCC (Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer) score identifies low-risk patients potentially suitable for oral antibiotics (e.g. ciprofloxacin + co-amoxiclav) and early discharge. A score ≥21 = low risk. Components include burden of illness, no hypotension, no COPD, solid tumour or no prior fungal infection, no dehydration, outpatient status, and age <60.

MASCC ≥21 = low risk. But it is a permission slip, not an order — the unwell patient stays in whatever the score says.

Escalation and the search for the hidden bug

  • Persistent fever at 48–72 h: re-examine, re-culture, image (CT chest for fungal nodules), consider line removal — do not just keep waiting.
  • Add antifungal cover (e.g. an echinocandin such as caspofungin, or liposomal amphotericin/voriconazole for suspected mould) in high-risk patients with persistent fever ≥4–7 days despite broad-spectrum antibiotics, or with positive fungal markers/CT signs (halo sign).
  • Consider resistant Gram-negatives and escalate to a carbapenem ± additional agents if not responding.

G-CSF — adjunct, not treatment

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor shortens neutropenia duration. It is used for secondary prophylaxis and in selected high-risk established febrile neutropenia (profound/prolonged neutropenia, pneumonia, hypotension, invasive fungal infection), but it is not a substitute for antibiotics and is not routinely given to every episode.

3 · 🛡️ Asplenia, hyposplenism & OPSI

The spleen is the body's filter for encapsulated organisms and the site of IgM memory B-cells. Lose it and you lose the ability to clear polysaccharide-encapsulated bacteria. The result is Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI) — a fulminant sepsis that can progress from a mild febrile illness to death within hours, with a mortality of up to 50%.

Causes of hyposplenism: surgical splenectomy, sickle cell disease (autosplenectomy), coeliac disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and post-radiation.

The classic OPSI organismsWhy they matter
Streptococcus pneumoniae~50–90% of OPSI — the dominant pathogen
Haemophilus influenzae type bEncapsulated; vaccine-preventable
Neisseria meningitidisEncapsulated; vaccine-preventable
Capnocytophaga canimorsusDog bites — ask about pets
Malaria / BabesiaMore severe without a spleen
💡 The asplenic sepsis bundle — SAVE

Standby Antibiotics (patient-held amoxicillin/co-amoxiclav to swallow at the first sign of infection before reaching hospital), Vaccination (pneumococcal PCV13+PPV23, Hib, MenACWY + MenB, annual influenza), and Education + a medical-alert card/bracelet. Many also take lifelong prophylactic penicillin V (or a macrolide if allergic), especially in the first 2 years, in children, and after prior OPSI.

⚠️ A febrile asplenic patient is a resuscitation call

Do not triage the febrile splenectomised patient to the waiting room. Give IV ceftriaxone immediately — treat every fever as incipient OPSI until proven otherwise. The window from "a bit unwell" to periarrest can be a couple of hours.

4 · 🧬 Transplant, biologics & steroids — the opportunists

Solid-organ and stem-cell transplant recipients, and patients on biologics (anti-TNF, rituximab, JAK inhibitors) or chronic corticosteroids (≥20 mg prednisolone for ≥2 weeks is a useful threshold for significant immunosuppression), have impaired cell-mediated immunity and blunted inflammatory signs. The timeline after transplant predicts the pathogen:

Post-transplant periodTypical pathogens
<1 monthNosocomial/surgical: line infections, wound, C. difficile, donor-derived
1–6 monthsOpportunistic: CMV, PCP (Pneumocystis), Aspergillus, Nocardia, reactivated TB, EBV/PTLD
>6 monthsCommunity pathogens + late opportunists in the heavily immunosuppressed
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP): insidious dyspnoea, hypoxia out of proportion to the chest film, raised LDH — treat with high-dose co-trimoxazole and add steroids if PaO₂ low. Prophylaxis prevents it.
  • CMV: fever, cytopenias, colitis, pneumonitis — send a CMV PCR.
  • Invasive aspergillosis: think in prolonged neutropenia and steroid users; CT halo/air-crescent sign, galactomannan; treat with voriconazole/isavuconazole.
  • Steroids mask the acute abdomen — a perforation may present with only a mild ache and a soft belly.
🎯 Ask the immunosuppression history every time

"What are you taking, and what have you had?" A drug history of anti-TNF, rituximab, or high-dose steroids, a transplant, a splenectomy scar, or recent chemotherapy completely reframes a "minor" fever. Reactivation risk (TB, hepatitis B, strongyloides) matters as much as new infection.

5 · 🎭 The deceptively well-looking patient

This is the trap that kills. The immunocompromised septic patient frequently has:

  • No fever (or hypothermia) — steroids and profound neutropenia blunt the pyrogenic response.
  • A normal or low white cell count — you cannot mount a leukocytosis with no marrow reserve.
  • No localising signs — no pus, no consolidation on X-ray, a soft abdomen despite perforation.
  • A brief window of normal observations before catastrophic, rapid decompensation.
Treat the immunocompromised patient's mild symptoms as a normal host's severe ones. Escalate on suspicion, not on physiology.
☠️ M&M — the neutropenic patient who "looked fine"

Our 41-year-old from the opening — 10 days post-chemotherapy, one reading of 38.1°C, walking and talking, observations near-normal. She waited 2 hours 40 minutes to be seen because the triage category was low; nobody had checked a full blood count on arrival, and the "she looks well" narrative held. Her ANC was 0.2. She had no neutrophils to make her look sick, no white cells to flag the count, and no signs to localise the source — a Gram-negative bacteraemia from gut mucositis was seeding unopposed. By the time antibiotics went up she was on noradrenaline; she survived only after 6 days of ICU. Lessons: in any patient on chemotherapy, fever plus a plausible immunocompromise is neutropenic sepsis until the count says otherwise; check the ANC immediately, give the anti-pseudomonal β-lactam within one hour, and never let "looks well" override the immune history. The reassuring appearance was the disease, not the reassurance.

6 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Broken defences hide the fire — no pus, no leukocytosis, blunted fever, and rapid collapse. Escalate on suspicion.
  2. Febrile neutropenia = fever + ANC <0.5 = emergency: anti-pseudomonal β-lactam (pip-tazobactam/meropenem/cefepime) within 1 hour, cultures must not delay the dose.
  3. Don't add vancomycin routinely — reserve it for instability, line infection, SSTI, severe mucositis, or MRSA. Add antifungals for persistent fever ≥4–7 days.
  4. MASCC ≥21 flags low-risk patients for possible oral therapy — but clinical judgement overrules the score.
  5. Asplenia → OPSI from encapsulated bugs: vaccinate, standby antibiotics, medic-alert, often lifelong penicillin; treat any fever as OPSI with immediate IV ceftriaxone.
  6. Transplant/biologic/steroid patients get opportunists (PCP, CMV, Aspergillus, Nocardia, TB reactivation) and mask acute abdomens — the timeline predicts the pathogen.
  7. Treat mild symptoms as severe disease — the deceptively well immunocompromised patient is the one who arrests.

moderatorQs.q: Define febrile neutropenia and state the single most time-critical action.
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Febrile neutropenia is a temperature >38.0°C (or a single reading ≥38.3°C) with an absolute neutrophil count <0.5 ×10⁹/L — or <1.0 and predicted to fall below 0.5. The single most time-critical action is empiric anti-pseudomonal β-lactam monotherapy within one hour of presentation — piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g, or meropenem/cefepime — and cultures must never delay the first dose. Fever may be the only sign; in profound neutropenia even fever can be absent, so hypotension, hypothermia or new confusion should trigger the same pathway. This is a Sepsis-Six-level emergency with an oncology label.

moderatorQs.q: When should you add a glycopeptide such as vancomycin to the empiric regimen?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Not routinely. IDSA is explicit that adding vancomycin to the initial empiric regimen for every febrile neutropenic patient does not improve outcomes and drives resistance and nephrotoxicity. Add a glycopeptide only for a specific indication: haemodynamic instability/severe sepsis, suspected central-line or catheter infection, skin/soft-tissue infection, severe mucositis, known MRSA colonisation, or Gram-positive cocci in blood cultures before sensitivities return. If added empirically, review at 48–72 h and stop it if no resistant Gram-positive organism is identified.

moderatorQs.q: Why is a mildly febrile asplenic patient a resuscitation-level emergency?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because the spleen is the filter for encapsulated organisms and the source of IgM memory B-cells; without it, a pneumococcal (or Hib/meningococcal) bacteraemia is uncontrolled and can progress from mild malaise to fatal Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI) within hours, with mortality up to 50%. S. pneumoniae causes the majority. The correct response to any fever in an asplenic patient is immediate IV ceftriaxone and full sepsis work-up — never the waiting room. Prevention wraps around vaccination, patient-held standby antibiotics, a medic-alert card, and often lifelong prophylactic penicillin.

audienceQs.q: How do I use the MASCC score to decide on oral antibiotics and discharge?
audienceQs.answerHTML: The MASCC score risk-stratifies febrile neutropenia; a score ≥21 identifies a low-risk patient who may be suitable for oral antibiotics (typically ciprofloxacin plus co-amoxiclav) and early or ambulatory management. Points come from low burden of illness, no hypotension, no COPD, a solid tumour or no previous fungal infection, no dehydration needing IV fluids, outpatient status at fever onset, and age <60. Crucially it is a permission slip, not a directive: any clinical concern — instability, comorbidity, poor social support, uncertain follow-up — keeps the patient in on IV therapy regardless of the number.

audienceQs.q: My splenectomy patient asks what they actually need long-term. What's the package?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Remember the bundle. Vaccination: pneumococcal (PCV13 then PPV23, with PPV23 boosters), Hib, MenACWY and MenB, and annual influenza. Standby antibiotics: a patient-held course of amoxicillin (or co-amoxiclav) to start at the first sign of infection and then seek urgent care. Prophylaxis: many take lifelong (or at least 2-year) prophylactic penicillin V — a macrolide if penicillin-allergic — especially in children and after previous OPSI. Plus a medic-alert card/bracelet, education that any fever means immediate assessment, and malaria precautions when travelling, since infection is more severe without a spleen.

audienceQs.q: A renal transplant patient on tacrolimus and prednisolone has breathlessness and hypoxia but a near-clear chest X-ray. What am I worried about?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) is high on the list — the hallmark is hypoxia out of proportion to the chest film, insidious exertional dyspnoea, a dry cough, and a raised LDH, classically 1–6 months post-transplant when cell-mediated immunity is most suppressed. Confirm with induced sputum or BAL PCR and treat with high-dose co-trimoxazole, adding corticosteroids if significantly hypoxic. Keep CMV pneumonitis and invasive aspergillosis in the differential (send CMV PCR and galactomannan), and remember steroids and immunosuppression blunt the signs, so treat early and image with CT rather than relying on a normal plain film.
